text:
Police figures show that the number of reported burglaries has fallen steadily for a decade, and many people credit new crime-prevention schemes. But surveys of households suggest that a large share of burglaries are never reported to the police. And over the same decade, the number of insurance claims for burglary has stayed roughly the same.
Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?
options: Burglary has fallen sharply in recent years.
Victims should be required by law to report burglaries.
Crime-prevention schemes have failed to reduce burglary.
Insurance claims are the best way to measure burglary.
The belief that burglary is steadily falling may not match what is really happening.
solution: Unreported burglaries and steady insurance claims both cast doubt on the falling police figures, so the claimed decline may not be real. The passage stops short of saying burglary has not fallen or that the schemes failed, proposes no law, and offers insurance claims as a reason for doubt, not as the best measure.

text:
Alcohol-free beer is now sold in most supermarkets. It tastes much like ordinary beer, and many drinkers buy it for that reason. The harm done by beer comes almost entirely from its alcohol, which damages the liver, impairs judgement and is linked to several cancers. Alcohol-free beer contains at most a trace of alcohol, and nothing else in it is known to be harmful.
Which one of the following is a conclusion which can be drawn from the above passage?
options: Alcohol-free beer is a relatively safe choice for people who enjoy the taste of beer.
Alcohol-free beer should be banned because it encourages drinking.
People dependent on alcohol can cure themselves by switching to alcohol-free beer.
Alcohol-free beer will make drinking more popular.
Brewers should stop making ordinary beer.
solution: If beer's harm comes from alcohol, and alcohol-free beer has almost none and nothing else harmful, it is a relatively safe alternative for those who like the taste. The passage gives no reason for a ban, makes no claim about curing dependence or about popularity, and does not recommend what brewers should do.

text:
A certain cooking fat takes up 5% more volume when it melts.
What volume of the solid fat must be melted to give exactly 210 cm³ of liquid fat?
solution: Melting multiplies the volume by 1.05, so the solid volume is 210 / 1.05 = 200 cm³. Taking 5% off 210 (199.5 cm³) is the trap: 5% of the smaller, solid volume is not the same as 5% of the liquid volume.

text:
In a fantasy game there are Zerks, Mons, Lops and Tibs. All Zerks are Mons. No Mons are Lops. Some Lops are Tibs.
Which one of the following is definitely NOT true?
solution: Every Zerk is a Mon, and no Mon is a Lop, so no Zerk can be a Lop: "Some Zerks are Lops" must be false. The others are possible: a Tib could be a Mon (only some Tibs are said to be Lops), Zerks might or might not be Tibs, there may be Mons that are not Zerks, and all Tibs could be Lops.

text:
Ben finishes school at 15:30. He will take the train home, spend 30 minutes getting his kit ready, then take the train to the swimming pool, where he needs 10 minutes to change before a session. Sessions start every 20 minutes from 16:40.

| school | 15:20 | 15:45 | 16:10 | 16:35 | 17:00 | 17:25 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| home | 15:40 | 16:05 | 16:30 | 16:55 | 17:20 | 17:45 |
| pool | 15:55 | 16:20 | 16:45 | 17:10 | 17:35 | 18:00 |

What is the earliest session he can join?
solution: The first train after 15:30 is the 15:45, reaching home at 16:05. He is ready at 16:35, so he misses the train passing home at 16:30 and takes the one at 16:55, reaching the pool at 17:10. After 10 minutes changing it is 17:20, which is a session time (16:40, 17:00, 17:20).

text:
Ten years ago the town library had 30 study desks, and a third of them were usually empty. Today it has 90 desks, and they are nearly always full. This may seem surprising when so much information is now online. Possible reasons include crowded student housing, unreliable home internet, the cost of heating a home all day and the library's longer opening hours.
Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?
options: The library is now the most popular place to study in the town.
Students work harder than they did ten years ago.
People will not study unless more desks are provided.
People are less willing to study at home than they were ten years ago.
More people study at the library now than ten years ago.
solution: About 20 desks were in use ten years ago, and about 90 are now, so more people study there. The passage lists only possible reasons, so it cannot conclude that people dislike studying at home or work harder, and it compares the library only with its own past, not with other places.

text:
A bathroom is 2.5 m high, 3 m wide and 5 m long. All four of its walls will be tiled, except for the doorway (2 m by 1 m) and two small openings (each 1 m by 0.5 m). One box of tiles covers 4 m².
How many boxes must be bought?
solution: Wall area: 2 x (3 + 5) x 2.5 = 40 m². Subtract the doorway (2 m²) and the openings (2 x 0.5 = 1 m²): 37 m². At 4 m² per box that is 9.25 boxes, so 10 must be bought. Forgetting to round up gives 9.

text:
About 1 person in 20 in a population has a certain condition. A screening test misses 10% of the people who have it (they test negative). Of all the people who test positive, 80% do not have the condition.
If a person tests negative, roughly what is the chance that they have the condition?
solution: Take 1000 people: 50 have the condition, of whom 45 test positive and 5 negative. Those 45 are only 20% of all positives, so there are 225 positives and 775 negatives. Of the 775 negatives, 5 have the condition: about 0.6%. 10% is the share of affected people the test misses, a different question.

text:
An old fridge draws 200 W whenever it runs. A new, efficient model draws 80 W but costs €180 more to buy. Electricity costs €0.30 per kWh.
After how many hours of running does the new fridge save enough on electricity to cover its extra price?
solution: The new fridge uses 120 W less: 0.12 kWh per hour, saving 0.12 x €0.30 = €0.036 an hour. €180 / €0.036 = 5000 hours. Using the new fridge's own 80 W instead of the 120 W saving gives 7500, and forgetting to change watts into kilowatts gives 5.

text:
Two years ago, Mia had four times as many stamps as Leo. Since then each of them has added 20 stamps to their collection, and now Mia has twice as many as Leo.
How many stamps does Mia have now?
solution: If Leo had x stamps two years ago, Mia had 4x. Now 4x + 20 = 2(x + 20), so 2x = 20 and x = 10. Mia had 40 and now has 60 (Leo has 30). 40 is her number two years ago.

text:
A café buys 200 kg of coffee beans at the start of each month. The price per kilogram from January to April was:

| | January | February | March | April |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| price per kg | €11.00 | €10.80 | €11.20 | €10.60 |

How much less would the café have spent if it had bought all 800 kg in April?

Bestseller lists for books are harder to compile than they used to be. Sales now include e-books and audiobooks as well as printed books in shops. And many books are read without being bought at all: they are borrowed from libraries or passed between friends. These readers do not appear in sales figures, so bestseller lists do not show which books are really the most read.
Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen this argument?
options: Borrowing and passing on books is much more common for some kinds of book than for others.
Combining shop and online sales into one list is straightforward.
It is legal to pass a book on to a friend.
Authors care more about sales than about how many people read their books.
Bestseller lists have never been completely accurate.
solution: If uncounted readers were spread evenly, the lists would still rank books correctly. If borrowing is far more common for some kinds of book, those books are undercounted relative to others, so the lists really do misrepresent what is most read. Easy compiling weakens the first point; legality, authors' motives and past inaccuracy do not bear on the claim.

text:
Working from home is often described as a new way of life brought about by the internet. Yet before the industrial revolution most people worked where they lived: farmers on their own land, weavers at looms in their cottages, and shopkeepers in rooms below the family home. It was the arrival of factories and offices that separated home from work.
Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion of the above passage?
options: Working from home will one day replace offices completely.
Working where one lives is not new; for most of history it was normal.
Most people today work from home.
The internet has made people more productive.
solution: The examples show that working at home was the usual pattern before factories and offices, so it is not a new way of life. The passage makes no prediction, gives no figures for today, passes no judgement on factories and says nothing about productivity.

text:
Many professional athletes struggle with money and with their mental health after they retire, often in their early thirties. Some blame coaches and agents, who earned a share of their winnings and pushed them to focus only on sport. The athletes who cope best are often those who kept studying during their careers or built up skills for another job.
Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?
options: Sport is a badly paid career.
Athletes who keep competing stay healthy.
Athletes should develop interests and skills that open up other careers.
Coaches should not be allowed to manage athletes' money.
There are few jobs for retired athletes.
solution: Those who cope best after retiring prepared for other work, so developing other interests and skills is the lesson the passage supports. It does not say sport pays badly, that competing keeps athletes healthy, that coaches should be banned from managing money, or that jobs are scarce.

text:
Vending machines in schools should sell only water and unsweetened drinks. Many pupils already take in far more sugar than is healthy, and sugary drinks are a major source of it, so removing them from schools is urgent.
Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens this argument?
options: Many pupils prefer sweet drinks to water.
A can of cola contains about seven teaspoons of sugar.
Schools earn money from their vending machines.
In schools that removed sugary drinks from their machines, pupils' total sugar intake fell rather than shifting to drinks bought elsewhere.
Many pupils bring drinks from home.
solution: The argument assumes that removing the drinks will cut pupils' sugar. Evidence that it did, and that pupils did not simply buy sugary drinks elsewhere, supports it directly. The sugar in a can is already implied, school income and drinks from home count against the policy's effect, and pupils' preferences do not show it would work.

text:
A grandmother shared some money among three grandchildren in the ratio 6 : 4 : 3. Later she gave an extra €8 to the grandchild who had received least, and now one share was the largest and the other two were equal.
How much did she give the three grandchildren altogether?
solution: Write the shares as 6k, 4k and 3k. Adding €8 to the smallest makes it equal to the middle one: 3k + 8 = 4k, so k = 8 and the shares were €48, €32 and €24, which is €104. With the extra €8 she gave €112 altogether. €104 forgets the extra €8.

text:
A cereal bar lists its ingredients in order of decreasing weight:
oats (45%), honey, raisins, almonds (12%), sunflower oil, salt
What is the largest percentage of honey the bar could contain?
solution: Oats take 45% and almonds 12%. Raisins come before almonds, so they are at least 12%. That leaves at most 100 - 45 - 12 - 12 = 31% for honey, with the oil and salt taking almost nothing. Ignoring the raisins' minimum gives 43%.

text:
Four children share a bag of sweets by taking 6 each, in turn, until the bag runs out. On the last turn there are not enough for Dan, the fourth child, to take 6. The other three then each give Dan 1 sweet, and all four end up with the same number.
How many sweets did Dan take on his last turn?
solution: If there were r full rounds before Dan's short turn, each of the other three has 6(r + 1) and Dan has 6r + d. After giving 1 each, they have 6r + 5, and Dan has 6r + d + 3. These are equal, so d = 2.

text:
Of 120 students, 70 study French, 50 study German and 25 study neither language.
How many study German but not French?
solution: 120 - 25 = 95 students study at least one language. 70 + 50 = 120 counts the students who study both twice, so 120 - 95 = 25 study both. German only = 50 - 25 = 25.

text:
A reservoir is at 40% of its capacity. A week of rain increases the amount of water in it by 30%. The same amount of rain is expected next week.
If that happens, what percentage of its capacity will the reservoir then hold?
solution: A 30% increase on 40% of capacity is 12% of capacity, bringing it to 52%. The same AMOUNT of rain next week adds another 12%: 64%. Increasing by 30% again (to 67.6%) wrongly assumes a bigger amount of rain.

text:
Four friends compare their heights:
1 Mira is shorter than Nola.
2 Pia is shorter than Quin.
3 Quin is taller than Nola.
If all three statements are true, which one of the following must also be true?
solution: From 1 and 3, Quin is taller than Nola, who is taller than Mira, so Quin is taller than Mira. Pia is only known to be shorter than Quin, so how she compares with Nola or Mira cannot be told; and 'Nola is taller than Quin' contradicts statement 3.

text:
These were the votes in a class election:

| name | Ana | Ben | Carla | Dev | Eva |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| votes | 45 | 35 | 60 | 15 | 25 |

When a pie chart of the results was drawn, one of these numbers was copied wrongly; the other four were copied correctly. The angles drawn were 112.5°, 90°, 67.5°, 52.5° and 37.5°.
Whose number was copied wrongly?
solution: The angles add up to 360°. Ana 45, Ben 35, Carla 60 and Eva 25 match 67.5°, 52.5°, 90° and 37.5° at 1.5° per vote, which means the chart was drawn for 360/1.5 = 240 votes. These four make 165, so the fifth number was taken as 75, giving 112.5°. Dev's 15 was copied as 75.

text:
A 12 km stretch of road takes a car 15 minutes to drive. The car travels at a steady 60 km/h, except through a section of roadworks where it is limited to 30 km/h.
How long is the section of roadworks?
solution: At 60 km/h the whole 12 km would take 12 minutes, so the roadworks add 3 minutes. Each kilometre at 30 km/h takes 2 minutes instead of 1, adding 1 minute per km, so the roadworks are 3 km long. Check: 9 km in 9 minutes plus 3 km in 6 minutes = 15 minutes.

text:
After an unusually wet summer, some people are saying that warnings about future droughts in the region are wrong. That conclusion cannot be drawn from one season. The drought warnings are about the long-term trend in rainfall, not about every single year. This summer's rain was caused by an unusual position of the jet stream, which pushed storms further south than normal.
Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen this argument?
options: Some of the people doubting the warnings live in areas that stayed dry this summer.
The summer before last had average rainfall.
Over the past twenty years, average summer rainfall in the region has fallen, even though some summers were wet.
All the people doubting the warnings live in areas that had a wet summer.
Further evidence supports the claim that the drought warnings are wrong.
solution: The argument says one wet season does not overturn a long-term trend. Evidence that the twenty-year average has fallen despite some wet summers shows exactly that. Where the doubters live does not affect the reasoning, one average summer tells us nothing about the trend, and further evidence against the warnings would weaken the argument.

text:
Lea lends money to friends every Monday, for either 1 or 2 weeks; each loan is repaid in full on the Monday it falls due, before she makes that day's loan. She starts with €100 and lends:

| week | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| amount lent | €40 | €30 | €25 |

What is the least money she could have on the Monday of week 3, after making that week's loan?
solution: To have the least, every loan should be out as long as possible. The week-1 loan lasts at most 2 weeks, so it is repaid on the Monday of week 3. The week-2 loan, if for 2 weeks, is still out, and the week-3 loan has just been made. So she holds €100 - €30 - €25 = €45. Treating all three loans as still out gives €5, which the 2-week limit makes impossible.

text:
Many shops leave their window displays lit all night. To save energy, they should switch them off after midnight. Very few people pass by after that time, and modern security cameras record clearly in low light.
Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen this argument?
options: Shop owners like their displays to be seen.
Window lighting is a small part of a shop's energy use.
Some passers-by feel safer in brightly lit streets.
Modern LED lights use much less energy than older bulbs.
In towns where shops already switch off their window lights at midnight, break-ins have not increased.
solution: The obvious objection is that dark shop fronts invite crime. Evidence that switching off has not increased break-ins answers it and supports the argument. A small share of energy use and efficient LEDs reduce the saving; owners' wishes and passers-by feeling safer are reasons against switching off.

text:
The knee-jerk reflex uses a stretch receptor in the thigh muscle, one sensory neurone and one motor neurone, with no relay neurone between them.
How many synapses does this reflex arc have inside the spinal cord?
solution: The sensory neurone synapses directly onto the motor neurone in the spinal cord: one synapse. The motor neurone's junction with the muscle is outside the central nervous system. A reflex with a relay neurone, like pulling a hand from a hot object, has two synapses in the cord.

text: Which of these molecules is built from the greatest number of different chemical elements?
solution: A nucleotide has a phosphate group (P), a sugar (C, H, O) and a nitrogenous base (N): five elements. Glucose, triglycerides and cellulose contain only C, H and O, and water only H and O.

text:
Which of these homeostatic responses are controlled through the hypothalamus?
1 sweating when the body is too hot
2 releasing less ADH when the blood is too dilute
3 releasing insulin when the blood glucose concentration rises
solution: The hypothalamus is the body's thermostat and also senses the water potential of the blood, controlling ADH release from the pituitary. Insulin release needs no brain: the beta cells of the pancreas detect the glucose concentration themselves and respond directly. 1 and 2 only.

text:
Shortly after a meal, which row names a vessel carrying blood with a very high concentration of oxygen, and a vessel carrying blood with the highest concentration of glucose absorbed from the gut?

| | very high oxygen | highest absorbed glucose |
|---|---|---|
| row 1 | pulmonary artery | hepatic vein |
| row 2 | vena cava | hepatic portal vein |
| row 3 | pulmonary artery | hepatic portal vein |
| row 4 | pulmonary vein | renal vein |
| row 5 | pulmonary vein | hepatic portal vein |
solution: The pulmonary vein carries blood just oxygenated in the lungs. Glucose absorbed in the small intestine goes straight to the liver in the hepatic portal vein, before the liver stores much of it; the hepatic vein carries blood after that. The pulmonary artery and vena cava carry deoxygenated blood.

text: Which enzyme carries out transcription, joining RNA nucleotides in an order set by a DNA template?
solution: RNA polymerase reads the template strand and links complementary RNA nucleotides into mRNA. DNA polymerase copies DNA during replication, ligase seals DNA backbones, reverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA, and ribosomes carry out translation.

text:
A cross produces offspring with four phenotypes in the ratio 1 : 1 : 1 : 1.
Which of the following could be true?
1 Two genes were studied, each with two alleles.
2 One parent was heterozygous for both genes and the other homozygous recessive for both.
3 Both parents were heterozygous for both genes.
solution: Four phenotypes from a cross fits two genes with two alleles each (1). The test cross AaBb x aabb gives AaBb, Aabb, aaBb and aabb in equal numbers: 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 (2). Two double heterozygotes give 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 instead (3 wrong). 1 and 2 only.

text: A skin cell and a liver cell are taken from the same healthy person. Which of the following would be the SAME in both?
options: the base sequence of their nuclear DNA
solution: Both cells come from the same zygote by mitosis, so their nuclear DNA is identical. They differ because they express different genes, so their mRNA, proteins and shapes differ.

text: Which statement about human gametes is NOT correct?
options: A sperm carries either an X or a Y chromosome.
An egg always carries an X chromosome.
They are made by mitosis in the testes and ovaries.
solution: Gametes are made by MEIOSIS, which halves the chromosome number from 46 to 23 (haploid). The mother has XX, so every egg has an X; the father has XY, so a sperm has either. Mitosis would keep 46 chromosomes.

text: Which statement about nerve impulses in humans is NOT true?
options: They travel along neurones as electrical signals.
They usually act faster than hormones.
They cross synapses by means of chemical neurotransmitters.
They are carried to their target organs in the blood plasma.
solution: Hormones travel in the blood; nerve impulses travel along neurones, as action potentials, to a precise target. Nervous responses are fast and brief, and they cross synapses chemically.

text:
Which of these processes move substances DOWN their concentration gradient?
1 diffusion
2 facilitated diffusion
3 active transport
solution: Simple and facilitated diffusion are both passive: they go from high to low concentration, the second through channel or carrier proteins. Active transport uses carrier proteins and ATP to move substances AGAINST the gradient. 1 and 2 only.

text: Which cross can produce offspring with the genotype aabb?
solution: An aabb child needs an a and a b from EACH parent. AaBb can give ab and aabb gives only ab, so aabb is possible (1 in 4). In the others one parent is AA or BB and must pass on a dominant allele, so aabb is impossible.

text: Why are many bacterial infections becoming harder to treat with antibiotics?
options: Bacteria learn to avoid antibiotics during an infection.
Bacteria carrying mutations that give resistance survive treatment and pass the resistance on.
Antibiotics lose their strength inside the body over the years.
Viruses carry resistance genes into human cells.
solution: This is natural selection. Random mutations make a few bacteria resistant; the antibiotic kills the rest, and the survivors multiply, so resistance spreads (and can pass between bacteria on plasmids). Patients do not become resistant, and bacteria do not learn; overuse and unfinished courses speed the selection up.

text:
A newly made protein is to be placed in the cell surface membrane. In which order does it pass through these structures?
1 Golgi apparatus
2 vesicle
3 rough endoplasmic reticulum
4 cell surface membrane
solution: The protein is made on ribosomes of the rough ER and enters it, travels to the Golgi apparatus to be modified and sorted, and leaves in a vesicle that fuses with the cell surface membrane, leaving the protein in it. The Golgi always comes after the ER.

text:
Which of the following increase when the parasympathetic nervous system is dominant ("rest and digest")?
1 heart rate
2 movement of food along the gut
3 secretion of saliva
solution: The parasympathetic system promotes digestion: it increases gut movement (peristalsis) and saliva flow. It SLOWS the heart, through the vagus nerve; speeding the heart is the job of the sympathetic system and adrenaline. 2 and 3 only.

text:
Which of the following statements about the O-H bonds INSIDE a water molecule is/are correct?
1 They are much stronger than the hydrogen bonds between water molecules.
2 They are polar.
3 They break when water boils.
solution: The O-H bonds are covalent and about twenty times stronger than hydrogen bonds (1). Oxygen is far more electronegative than hydrogen, so they are polar, which is what makes hydrogen bonding possible (2). Boiling separates molecules by breaking hydrogen bonds; the water molecules themselves stay whole (3 wrong).

text: Which formula could NOT belong to a saturated, open-chain carboxylic acid?
solution: These acids fit \(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n}O_2}\): the C=O in the COOH group costs two hydrogens compared with an alkane. \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O_2}\) has two hydrogens too many for that (it fits a diol such as butane-1,4-diol). The others fit: ethanoic, propanoic, pentanoic and hexanoic acid.

text:
Which of the following statements about dissolving in water is/are correct?
1 Some ionic compounds, such as calcium carbonate, are insoluble in water.
2 Some covalent compounds, such as sucrose, dissolve in water.
3 Gases usually become less soluble in water as the temperature rises.
solution: Not every ionic solid dissolves: the lattice of calcium carbonate is too strong. Polar covalent molecules that can hydrogen-bond, like sucrose, dissolve well. Gases escape as water warms, which is why warm water holds less oxygen. All three are correct.

text:
Which substances are the REDUCING agents in these three reactions?
\(\mathrm{2Na + Cl_2 \rightarrow 2NaCl}\)
\(\mathrm{Zn + Cu^{2+} \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + Cu}\)
\(\mathrm{Cl_2 + 2Br^- \rightarrow 2Cl^- + Br_2}\)
solution: A reducing agent gives electrons away and is itself oxidised. Sodium goes from 0 to +1, zinc from 0 to +2, and bromide from -1 to 0 in bromine. Chlorine and \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) gain electrons, so they are the oxidising agents.

text: Which statement about lithium, sodium and potassium is NOT correct?
options: They react with water to form hydroxides.
They form ions with a 1+ charge.
They are soft enough to cut with a knife.
Their reactivity increases down the group.
They are all denser than water.
solution: Lithium, sodium and potassium all float on water (densities about 0.53, 0.97 and 0.86 g/cm3). The other statements are typical Group 1 properties: a single outer electron, lost more easily down the group, and weak metallic bonding that makes them soft.

text:
How many hydrogen atoms are in 0.32 g of methane, \(\mathrm{CH_4}\)?
[Relative atomic masses: H = 1; C = 12; Avogadro constant = \(6.0 \times 10^{23} \mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)]
solution: \(M_r\) of methane = 16, so 0.32 g is 0.020 mol of molecules. Each has four hydrogens: 0.080 mol of H atoms = \(0.080 \times 6.0 \times 10^{23} = 4.8 \times 10^{22}\). \(1.2 \times 10^{22}\) counts molecules, not hydrogen atoms.

text:
How many electrons does each ion in magnesium oxide have?
[Atomic numbers: O = 8; Mg = 12]
solution: Magnesium loses two electrons to form \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\): 12 - 2 = 10. Oxygen gains two to form \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\): 8 + 2 = 10. Both end with the neon arrangement.

text: Which is correct about the first and second ionisation energies of magnesium?
options: first: endothermic; second: smaller than the first
first: endothermic; second: endothermic and larger than the first
solution: Pulling an electron away from a nucleus always takes energy, so every ionisation energy is endothermic. The second electron leaves a 1+ ion that holds its remaining electrons more tightly, so the second ionisation energy is larger (about 1450 against 740 kJ/mol for magnesium).

text:
Consider these reactions:
\(\mathrm{C_2H_4 + Br_2 \rightarrow C_2H_4Br_2}\)
\(\mathrm{HCl + NaOH \rightarrow NaCl + H_2O}\)
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH \rightarrow C_2H_4 + H_2O}\)
Which type of reaction is NOT shown?
solution: Bromine adds across ethene's double bond (addition); an acid and a base form a salt and water (neutralisation); ethanol loses water to form ethene, which is both elimination and dehydration. No atom or group is swapped for another, so there is no substitution.

text:
Which rows correctly state whether the compound fizzes, giving carbon dioxide, when added to sodium carbonate solution?

| | compound | gives carbon dioxide |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ethanoic acid | yes |
| 2 | ethanol | no |
| 3 | ethanal | yes |
solution: Carboxylic acids are acidic enough to react with carbonates and release carbon dioxide, so ethanoic acid fizzes (row 1 correct). Alcohols and aldehydes are not acidic, so neither ethanol nor ethanal does: row 2 is correct and row 3 is wrong. This is the standard test for a COOH group.

text: Which is NOT the correct formula of a calcium compound?
solution: Calcium forms \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\), so it needs two 1- ions such as nitrate: calcium nitrate is \(\mathrm{Ca(NO_3)_2}\). Carbonate and sulfate are 2-, so one of each; phosphate is 3-, so three calciums balance two phosphates.

subject: Mathematics
text: For which values of \(x\) are both \(x^2 > 4\) and \(3 - x > 0\) true?
solution: \(x^2 > 4\) holds outside -2 and 2: \(x < -2\) or \(x > 2\). \(3 - x > 0\) means \(x < 3\). Combining: all of \(x < -2\) survives, and of \(x > 2\) only \(2 < x < 3\). Forgetting the negative branch gives just \(2 < x < 3\).

subject: Physics
text:
A student finds the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water by keeping water boiling with a heater of known power and measuring how much boils away.
Which of the following does the student NOT need?
options: the time for which the water boils
the temperature of the water before it was heated
the mass of water when timing starts
the mass of water when timing stops
solution: Latent heat = energy / mass boiled away. Energy = power x time, and the mass boiled away is the difference between the masses at the start and end of timing, while the water is already boiling. How cold the water was before it reached 100 °C does not enter the calculation.

subject: Physics
text:
Water is boiling steadily at 100 °C and atmospheric pressure. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
1 It absorbs energy but its temperature stays the same.
2 Hydrogen bonds between water molecules are broken.
3 O-H bonds inside the water molecules are broken.
solution: During a change of state the energy goes into separating molecules (latent heat), not into raising the temperature (1). Separating water molecules means breaking the hydrogen bonds between them (2). The molecules themselves survive as \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) in the steam (3 wrong).

subject: Physics
text:
A coil of superconducting wire has zero electrical resistance. A steady current flows in it.
Which statement is correct?
options: No magnetic field forms around the coil.
A large voltage is needed to keep the current flowing.
Energy is lost from the wire as heat at a rate of \(I^2R\).
A magnetic field forms around the coil, but no heat is produced in the wire.
solution: Heating is \(I^2R\), which is zero when R is zero, and with no resistance no voltage is needed to keep a steady current going. But any current produces a magnetic field, which is why superconducting coils are used for the strong magnets in MRI scanners.

subject: Physics
text: Which one of the following IS a vector quantity?
solution: A vector has a direction as well as a size. Momentum is mass x velocity, and velocity has a direction, so momentum does too. Kinetic energy, temperature, mass and power have size only: they are scalars.

subject: Mathematics
text: Simplify \(\ln(x^3y^2) - 3\ln(xy) + \ln y\).
solution: Expand: \(3\ln x + 2\ln y - 3\ln x - 3\ln y + \ln y\). The \(\ln x\) terms cancel, and \(2 - 3 + 1 = 0\), so the \(\ln y\) terms cancel too: the expression is 0 for all positive \(x\) and \(y\).

subject: Mathematics
text:
In a class, exactly \(\tfrac{3}{4}\) of the students play a sport and exactly \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) learn a musical instrument.
What is the range of possible values for the fraction of the class who do both?
solution: At most, every musician also plays a sport: \(\tfrac{1}{2}\). At least, the two groups overlap as little as possible, but together they make \(\tfrac{5}{4}\) of a class, so at least \(\tfrac{3}{4} + \tfrac{1}{2} - 1 = \tfrac{1}{4}\) must do both. \(\tfrac{3}{8}\) is the value only if the two are independent.

subject: Mathematics
text: Which of these points lies at a different distance from the line (y = x + 1) than the other four?
solution: The distance from \((p, q)\) to \(x - y + 1 = 0\) is \(\dfrac{|p - q + 1|}{\sqrt{2}}\). The numerators: (0, 3) gives 2, (2, 1) gives 2, (4, 3) gives 2, (1, 0) gives 2, but (3, 3) gives 1. So (3, 3) is the odd one out.

subject: Physics
text:
A 60 kg woman puts her whole weight on one stiletto heel, whose tip has an area of 1.0 cm².
What pressure does the heel exert on the floor?
[Take \(g = 10\) N/kg.]
solution: Weight = 60 x 10 = 600 N. Area: 1.0 cm² = \(1.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2\) (a centimetre is \(10^{-2}\) m, so a square centimetre is \(10^{-4}\)). Pressure = 600 / \(10^{-4}\) = \(6.0 \times 10^{6}\) Pa, more than an elephant's foot exerts.
